planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; the tricolor variegation is most vivid with at least six hours of direct sun, though the plant tolerates light shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and prune lightly right after the spring flower flush to keep the rounded habit tidy without sacrificing next year's buds. Rainbow Sensation is a Bailey Nurseries First Editions introduction grown chiefly for its three-tone variegated foliage, which shifts from dark green through pink to creamy yellow across the growing season, with dense clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers adding a second season of interest in late spring. Its compact, rounded form suits foundation plantings and mixed borders, and established plants are drought-tolerant once rooted in. Watch for any shoots that revert to solid green and prune them out at the base, since reverted growth is more vigorous and can overtake the variegated wood.

common_name: Bubbly Wine Weigela (Yellow-and-Green Variegated Compact Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; strong light brings out the brightest yellow-and-green variegation and the darkest burgundy stem color.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest foliage color and heaviest bloom. Bubbly Wine is a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction that opens fresh yellow-and-green variegated foliage in spring, holds that two-tone color through summer, and develops dark burgundy stems as the season progresses, with light purple-pink, bell-shaped flowers scattered across the compact, multi-stemmed mound in late spring. Its small mature size makes it useful for edging, low hedges, or container plantings where larger weigelas would overwhelm the space. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain shape, since flower buds form on the previous season's wood.

common_name: Vinho Verde Weigela (Lime-Green Foliage Weigela with Dark Edges)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; strongest sun produces the sharpest contrast between the lime-green leaf centers and their dark, almost black margins.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun for the best foliage contrast and bloom. Vinho Verde is a Proven Winners ColorChoice weigela notable for two-tone leaves with lime-green centers edged in a thick, dark brownish-black band, paired with dark reddish-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring. The compact, rounded habit fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and containers where its distinctive foliage color reads well against greener companions. Prune lightly right after the main bloom flush to maintain shape without removing next year's flower buds.

common_name: Very Fine Wine Weigela (Improved Compact Dark-Foliage Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; foliage color and bloom count are both strongest with at least six hours of direct sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and prune lightly right after the main spring flush to keep the compact mound tidy. Very Fine Wine is a Proven Winners ColorChoice weigela bred as an improved successor to the original Fine Wine, retaining the same cold hardiness and dwarf habit while offering darker burgundy-purple foliage and heavier flowering, with clusters of bright pink, trumpet-shaped blooms in late spring that draw hummingbirds. Its small, tidy size suits foundation plantings, low borders, and mixed containers. Established plants are drought-tolerant and need only an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to stay vigorous.

common_name: Ruby Queen Weigela (Compact Purple-Flushed Foliage Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; strong light brings out the deepest purple-red flush on new foliage.

directions: Ruby Queen was bred in Boskoop, the Netherlands, from a cross using Victoria weigela as the seed parent, and forms a compact, bushy, rounded shrub with narrow, dark green leaves flushed red to purple, most intensely when young. Funnel-shaped, rose-pink flowers open from late spring into summer, giving a longer bloom window than many one-flush weigelas. Its neat, smaller-than-Victoria habit works well in mixed borders or foundation plantings where a purple-tinged weigela is wanted without the larger footprint of older selections. Prune immediately after the main flowering flush to shape it, since blooms form on the previous season's wood.

common_name: Citrus Swizzle Forsythia (Variegated Dwarf Greenstem Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; strong light produces the clearest lime-green, cream, and white leaf variegation.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Citrus Swizzle arose as a branch sport of the dwarf 'Bronxensis' greenstem forsythia, discovered at a Wisconsin nursery, and is grown chiefly for its serrated leaves, which open with lime-green centers and chartreuse margins that fade toward creamy white and white as the season progresses. Like its parent it forms a low, dense, spreading mound and produces only a light scattering of small pale-yellow flowers in early spring, well before it leafs out into its main foliage display. Its compact size and slow growth suit it to rock gardens, low borders, or foreground plantings; remove any shoots that revert to solid green as soon as they appear.

common_name: Spring Fling Forsythia (University of Minnesota Cold-Hardy Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Spring Fling was bred at the University of Minnesota specifically for reliable flower-bud survival through harsh northern winters.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom. Spring Fling was developed and released by the University of Minnesota as a cold-hardy border forsythia whose flower buds tolerate harsh northern winters that routinely kill the buds of common border cultivars, so it reliably covers itself top to bottom in brilliant yellow flowers in early spring. The vigorous, upright shrub matures into a large informal specimen or hedge and adapts to a wide range of well-drained soils once established. Prune immediately after flowering to shape or control size, since old wood carries next year's flower buds and later pruning sacrifices bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; full sun produces the cleanest cream-white leaf variegation.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Discovery arose as a naturally occurring branch mutation found on an unnamed border forsythia and was introduced through the Hillier Collection in the United Kingdom, valued for its elegant foliage broadly edged in cream-white against a green center, held on a tidy, compact habit smaller than typical border forsythia. Deep yellow flowers open on bare stems in early spring ahead of the variegated foliage, giving two distinct seasons of interest. Watch for shoots that revert to solid green and remove them at the base promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and can overtake the variegated wood if left unchecked.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Ottawa was selected at the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa for its extreme flower-bud hardiness in zone 3-4 winters.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom. Ottawa is a hardy selection of Korean forsythia made at Canada's Central Experimental Farm, chosen for flowering earlier and more heavily than typical seed-grown Forsythia ovata, with flower buds tough enough to survive prairie and northern winters that damage the buds of common border forsythia. It later served as a parent in breeding the widely grown Northern Gold forsythia. The upright, rounded shrub is more compact than large border cultivars, making it useful where a smaller, dependably blooming forsythia is wanted in cold climates. Prune immediately after flowering, since next year's buds form on the current season's wood.
